evidence.source: Shuowen.org, transcribing Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai's annotation
evidence.field: 吃 entry: definition, structure, fanqie
evidence.text: The entry defines 吃 as difficult or halting speech and analyzes it as 从口气聲; it gives 居乙切. Duan Yucai repeats the structure and assigns the word to his fifteenth rhyme division.
evidence.title: 說文解字「吃」

evidence.source: 漢典 (ZDIC), citing Shuowen, Shiji and Hanshu
evidence.field: 吃 entry: early cited uses and historical phonology
evidence.text: The dictionary gives the stammer sense, citing Shuowen and the biographical histories' descriptions of Han Fei and Zhou Chang. It records the Guangyun category as 見母, 迄韻, entering tone, 居乙切; this is dictionary phonological classification, not a direct date for the character's formation.
evidence.title: 吃 chī - 漢典

evidence.source: Shiji Online, text of Shiji, Laozi Hanfei liezhuan
evidence.field: Han Fei biography: attested sense
evidence.text: The transmitted text says 韓非為人口吃，不能道說，而善著書, describing Han Fei as a stammerer who could not speak persuasively but wrote well. Shiji is a Han-dynasty compilation; this supports the early stammer sense, not an eating sense for 吃.
evidence.title: 老子韩非列传 — 《史记》列传第63篇

evidence.source: 桂馥, 說文解字義證, transcribed by 识典古籍
evidence.field: 吃 commentary: early textual citations and historical lexicography
evidence.text: The commentary gathers older citations for the stammer sense, including the Shiji Han Fei passage, the Hanshu Zhou Chang passage and Guanzi. Its discussion distinguishes these speech-related uses from later eating glosses; it is a Qing evidentiary commentary, not itself an early attestation.
evidence.title: 卷五-说文解字义证全文原文-识典古籍

evidence.source: 中央研究院, 漢字資料庫
evidence.field: 吃 entry: meanings, readings and graphic record availability
evidence.text: The database lists readings including chi1, ji2, qi1 and several regional romanizations, and distinguishes senses for halting speech, slow or difficult action, swallowing food or drink, swallowing chess pieces, absorbing, consuming and undergoing. Its separate historical-shape records for 吃 list Shuowen and later script materials; the ancient-inscription datasets shown on the page are not publicly available there, so this page does not establish an oracle-bone or bronze form for 吃.
evidence.title: 漢字「吃」：基本資料

evidence.source: 漢典 (ZDIC)
evidence.field: 吃 entry: shape history and literary references
evidence.text: The page displays Shuowen, clerical and regular-script categories, and identifies a Western Han Wuwei manuscript example for clerical 吃. It cites Shiji and Hanshu for stammering. Its listed eating history includes a passage from Jia Yi's Xinshu, but this attribution conflicts with a 2025 scholarly account that regards the Xinshu passage's graph as an unreliable early 喫 example; the attribution should not be treated as settled without inspecting the manuscript/textual transmission.
evidence.title: 吃 chī - 漢典

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 吃 entry: readings, senses and documentary examples
evidence.text: The dictionary gives the Shuowen definition and sound component 气, notes that the modern right side is written like 乞, and records jí for the speech-difficulty sense and chī for swallowing food or drink. It cites Shiji and Hanshu for the former and a Ming military manual for the latter; it treats eating as same as 喫. Those citations support differentiated sense histories, though they do not by themselves settle the graphic mechanism by which 吃 came to write the eating word.
evidence.title: [A00510] 吃 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 喫 entry: Shuowen supplement and dated use citations
evidence.text: The dictionary says 喫 is absent from the main Shuowen text but present in its later-added supplement with the gloss 'to eat' and structure 从口, [phonetic component] 聲. It cites the Southern Song-era Shishuo Xinyu tradition for a meat-eating example, Du Fu for an eighth-century example, and Yuan texts for 'suffer/endure.' These dates apply to the cited textual works or compositions, not necessarily the surviving manuscript forms.
evidence.title: [B00373] 喫 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Sichuan University Institute for Chinese Folk Culture Studies, report on Jiang Jicheng's lecture
evidence.field: 喫 origins and chronology: modern specialist account
evidence.text: The 2025 report says Jiang places early 喫 examples in Three Kingdoms Buddhist translations, initially with 'drink' and under Wu-dialect influence; it lists later Eastern Jin/Six Dynasties eating uses, including Shishuo Xinyu and Qimin Yaoshu. It reports his view that Tang poems and Dunhuang transformation texts show 喫 expanding into colloquial 'eat/drink,' with Northern colloquial use replacing 食 as a verb by the Five Dynasties. Jiang argues a relation of sound recording and later semantic differentiation involving 毄/喫/齧. This is a reported scholarly analysis and chronology, not a direct paleographic demonstration of the 吃 graph's development.
evidence.title: 〖项楚学术讲座〗蒋冀骋：“喫”字的来源和读音演变

evidence.source: Taiwan Academic Journal Open Access platform; Chen Songlin, article abstract
evidence.field: 吃 and 喫: competing account of graphic relationship
evidence.text: Chen's 2013 abstract proposes that eating 吃 arose as a simplification of 齕 and became homographic with speech 吃, while 喫 arose from simplification of 齧; he attributes interchange to sound borrowing between 乞 and 契. This differs from simpler dictionary descriptions of 喫 as an alternate graph or later replacement. The article page exposes only the abstract in the inspected content, so its detailed evidence was not reviewed.
evidence.title: 「吃」和「喫」的文字語義關係 / The Study of 喫 and 吃

evidence.source: 中央研究院, 漢字資料庫
evidence.field: 乞 entry: historical forms and account of relation to 气
evidence.text: The database reports 乞 and 气 as originally the same three-line graph for cloud/breath qi, with forms differentiated graphically; it says the later separated 乞 form came to represent begging after 气 specialized for air. Its displayed shape records include oracle-bone, bronze and small-seal categories. This is an account of 乞/气 history, not evidence that 吃 itself had an oracle-bone form.
evidence.title: 漢字「乞」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢典 (ZDIC), phonology references for 乞
evidence.field: 乞 historical pronunciation and phonetic relationship
evidence.text: The page reports Zhengzhang-style Old Chinese reconstructions for 乞 as *kʰɯds and *kʰɯd, and its Guangyun entry as 溪母, 迄韻, entering tone, with fanqie 去迄切. It labels an additional *kʰɯd reading as an air/breath-related form corresponding to 气. This gives historical phonological context for the component; it does not make 乞's modern Mandarin qǐ identical to 吃's chī.
evidence.title: 乞的音韻方言

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003)
evidence.field: 吃 phonology and component comparison
evidence.text: The entry gives Standard Mandarin 吃 chī and a regional/older jí reading, Guangyun 居乙切 in the 見母 迄韻 entering-tone category, and Zhengzhang Old Chinese 吃 *kɯd versus 乞 *kʰɯds/*kʰɯd. In that reconstruction the consonant and tone/ending distinctions are not identical, but the forms are compatible with a historical phonetic series. This supports a phonetic role, not a meaning contribution from 'begging.'
evidence.title: 吃 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.source: Shuowen.cn, transcribing Shuowen and Duan Yucai
evidence.field: 口 entry: graphic and semantic characterization
evidence.text: 口 is explained as what a person uses to speak and eat, and classified as pictographic in Shuowen. The page supplies a progression of 口 examples from oracle-bone and late Shang bronze through Warring States, Qin/Han clerical, Eastern Han stele and regular script. This supports 口's independent meaning and history, not an inference about the whole 吃 compound's earliest form.
evidence.title: 口字说文解字在线查询

evidence.source: 漢字ペディア, Japan Kanji Aptitude Testing Foundation
evidence.field: 吃 Japanese readings and senses
evidence.text: The entry gives on-reading キツ and kun-readings どもる, くう and すう; it glosses stammering and drinking/eating/sucking, and says some eating uses can be rewritten 喫. This documents modern Japanese readings, not the historical origin or date of the Japanese kun-reading.
evidence.title: 吃 | 漢字一字 | 漢字ペディア

evidence.source: Kotobank, 精選版 日本国語大辞典
evidence.field: 吃る Japanese kun-reading attestation
evidence.text: The dictionary dates its earliest example for Japanese どもる written 吃る to the 1420 Oeibon Rongo-shō, in a sentence describing halting speech. This is a dated Japanese lexical example, not evidence that the graph was created in Japan; no such origin claim was found.
evidence.title: 吃る(ドモル)とは？ 意味や使い方

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, transcribing Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai’s annotation
evidence.field: 吃 entry: definition, structure, fanqie
evidence.text: The entry defines 吃 as speech that is difficult or halting and analyzes it as 从口气聲; it gives 居乙切. This directly supports the traditional sound-component analysis and speech sense, but does not establish the compound’s earliest surviving artifact form.
evidence.title: 說文解字「吃」

evidence.source: 中央研究院, 漢字資料庫
evidence.field: 乞 entry: shape history and account of relation to 气
evidence.text: This database describes 乞 and 气 as historically sharing a three-line graph associated with cloud/breath, later differentiated in shape and use. It displays oracle-bone, bronze and small-seal categories for 乞. This evidence concerns the component’s history; it does not prove an oracle-bone 吃 form or trace the exact shape used in 吃.
evidence.title: 漢字「乞」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢典 (ZDIC), phonology references for 乞
evidence.field: 乞 historical pronunciation and Guangyun classification
evidence.text: The page gives Zhengzhang-style Old Chinese *kʰɯds and *kʰɯd for 乞, and Guangyun 去迄切, 溪母, 迄韻, entering tone. It notes the relationship to 气. These are historical pronunciation records for 乞, not proof that its modern Mandarin qǐ equals 吃 chī.
evidence.title: 乞的音韻方言

evidence.source: 漢典 (ZDIC), 吃 entry
evidence.field: 吃 entry: readings, cited senses, historical forms
evidence.text: The entry records Mandarin chī for eating/drinking and jí for halting speech, and cites the Shiji description of Han Fei as 口吃. It reproduces the Shuowen analysis 从口气聲 and Guangyun category 居乙切. The shape examples listed include a Shuowen small-seal form and a Western Han Wuwei manuscript clerical example. These data do not date the character’s original formation; its Xinshu eating citation is not sufficient to settle the earliest eating spelling.
evidence.title: 吃 chī - 漢典

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 吃 entry: structure, differentiated readings and dated citations
evidence.text: The dictionary repeats the Shuowen structure 从口，气聲 and says the modern right side is written like 乞. It distinguishes jí for difficult speech, citing Shuowen, Guanzi and Shiji, from chī for eating/drinking, treated as equivalent to 喫 and supported by later citations including a Ming military manual. It also marks ancient-inscription datasets as unavailable on the page; no early oracle-bone or bronze 吃 form can be established from it.
evidence.title: [A00510] 吃 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003)
evidence.field: 吃 and 乞 Old Chinese comparison
evidence.text: The entry gives Mandarin 吃 chī, a jí reading, Guangyun 居乙切, and Zhengzhang Old Chinese 吃 *kɯd versus 乞 *kʰɯds/*kʰɯd. In that reconstruction system, the forms are similar enough to be compatible with a phonetic-series relation, though they are not identical. Together with Shuowen’s explicit 聲 analysis, this supports phonetic use; it does not show that 乞 contributes the meaning ‘beg.’
evidence.title: 吃 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.source: 书法图集, 吃 shape-history page
evidence.field: 吃: displayed historical shape examples
evidence.text: The page labels shape examples as a Warring States Qi ceramic inscription (陶彙3.1034), a Shuowen mouth-section form, and a Western Han Wuwei manuscript clerical form. These are useful reported form-history leads but the page is not an excavated artifact catalogue, and the images themselves have no reuse statement visible in the inspected text. Treat the artifact identifications as candidates requiring source-level verification.
evidence.title: 吃字形演变_吃的甲骨文_吃的金文_吃字篆文_写法_吃字源图片

evidence.source: Wikimedia Commons file description
evidence.field: 吃 regular-script example and reuse rights
evidence.text: The Commons page describes a modern regular-script 吃 character in a nine-square grid, uploaded in 2012 as the uploader’s own work and released to the public domain (also listing GFDL). It is a modern specimen, not an ancient artifact or historical form, so it is not useful for explaining the character’s development.

gaps: No inspected primary paleographic evidence established the earliest form of the whole 吃 graph or a dated oracle-bone/bronze 吃 attestation. The available Sinica 吃 page lists script-history sources but marks key ancient-character corpora unavailable; no glyph image was visually inspected.

The component analysis is directly attested in Shuowen as 从口气聲, and modern right-side 乞 is documented, but the exact graphic path from 气 to the positional form 乞 in 吃 was not independently traced through dated 吃 witnesses. The database's 乞/气 history is adjacent evidence, not a complete 吃 evolution sequence.

The earliest eating use is disputed in the inspected sources. The 2025 report places early 喫 use in Three Kingdoms Buddhist translations and rejects the often-cited Xinshu passage as an early example; dictionaries and another scholarly abstract offer different histories. Full scholarly argument and original manuscript witnesses were not inspected, so no single graphic ancestry or precise earliest date is asserted.

The relation between the speech word 吃 and eating 喫/吃 remains unresolved: evidence supports distinct senses and later interchange, while sources disagree about phonetic borrowing, simplification, and which graph supplied the eating spelling. Sense chronology must not be inferred from dictionary ordering.

The phonetic-series claim is supported by Shuowen's sound-component statement and the cited reconstruction comparison, but the evidence does not establish any semantic contribution from 乞's begging sense. No actual object-naming or whole-graph loan hypothesis is proposed, so that kind of borrowing chain is inapplicable.

The 口 semantic contribution is a reasonable reading of the compound supported by the mouth radical and Shuowen's phonetic analysis; no separate source establishes exactly how the speech sense arose from that graphic semantic component.

Japanese dictionaries attest modern キツ and どもる and date a 1420 textual example, but the route and date by which this Chinese graph/reading entered Japanese, and the source of the native kun-reading, were not established.

The extant-text dates reported for Shiji, Hanshu, Shishuo Xinyu and Du Fu are not dates for the surviving physical witnesses. The reviewed sources did not provide manuscript-level dating for those quoted graph forms.

No inspected primary paleographic source established the earliest physical attestation of the whole 吃 graph. Reports of a Warring States Qi ceramic form and a Western Han Wuwei manuscript form remain leads; the cited Sinica and Taiwan database pages indicate that key ancient datasets are unavailable there.

Shuowen explicitly analyzes 吃 as 从口气聲. The later right-side form resembles 乞, and Sinica discusses 乞/气 history, but the precise dated graphic path from 气 to the positional component in 吃 was not traced.

The standard phonetic claim does not require a whole-graph loan theory. No evidence inspected here establishes that 乞 contributes meaning through ‘begging’; no source-word/object-name borrowing chain is proposed.

Earliest eating use and the relationship among 吃, 喫, 齕 and related forms remain disputed in the dossier’s cited accounts. Dictionary gloss order and the Xinshu citation alone cannot settle a chronology or graphic ancestry. The received Shiji speech example supports the stammer sense, not an eating sense.

The selected Wikimedia Commons image is modern regular script, not a historical glyph; the directly relevant historical form candidates found were on a page without a visible reuse license. Therefore no historical glyph image candidate is proposed: searches did not establish both a usable direct image URL and reuse provenance for an identified 吃 historical form.
No reviewed source dates the physical witness for the literary citations; composition/transmission dates should not be treated as artifact dates.
